hints: Focus on what particles sit in the lattice, discrete small molecules held by weak forces means simple molecular.
Sort each name into its family: ionic, metallic, giant covalent, or molecular, starting with calcium fluoride and nickel.
Remember sulfur exists as separate puckered rings that stack together with only weak London forces between them.
walkthrough:
**Recall the simple molecular model**

Think of tiny separate molecules packed together like marbles in a box. They are held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{simple molecular} = \text{discrete molecules} + \text{weak London forces}$$

**Test the first three solids**

Calcium fluoride, $\text{CaF}_2$, is ions ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{F}^-$) in a giant ionic lattice. Nickel, $\text{Ni}$, is positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, so metallic.

Silicon(IV) oxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, looks like $\text{CO}_2$ but do not be fooled. It is a giant covalent network of Si-O bonds, very hard with a very high melting point.

**Confirm sulfur**

Solid sulfur is made of separate $\text{S}_8$ crown-shaped molecules. There are no giant ionic, metallic or covalent bonds between these rings, only weak van der Waals forces.

Conclusion:
$$\text{S}_8 \text{ molecules + weak forces = simple molecular lattice}$$

options.A: Incorrect. Calcium fluoride, $\text{CaF}_2$, has a giant ionic lattice of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{F}^-$ ions held by strong electrostatic attraction. It has high melting point and conducts when molten, not the low melting soft properties of a simple molecular solid.
options.B: Incorrect. Nickel is a transition metal with metallic bonding, a lattice of $\text{Ni}$ cations in delocalised electrons. This gives high melting point, strength and electrical conductivity, the opposite of a simple molecular lattice.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the classic trap. Silicon(IV) oxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, is not simple molecular like $\text{CO}_2$. It forms a giant covalent (macromolecular) network with continuous Si-O single bonds, so it is very hard with a very high melting point.
options.D: Correct. Sulfur is made of discrete $\text{S}_8$ molecules packed in a lattice held together only by weak London dispersion forces. This is exactly a simple molecular lattice, giving low melting point and softness and no electrical conductivity.
